Part I: Why the AFFO Method Can Value APLD Higher Than the Revenue Method The AFFO method can produce a higher valuation for APLD than a revenue-multiple approach because: • EQIX's AFFO multiple (~30×) is structurally richer than its revenue multiple (~10×). • AFFO captures the recurring cash-generating power and high visibility of long-term, contracted hyperscale leases. • APLD's current development phase is highly capital intensive, but once its major campuses are substantially built and mature, the business should become relatively capital-light on a sustaining-capex basis. At that point, its economic profile should become increasingly similar to a mature data-center REIT, making AFFO a more relevant valuation metric. More....

Author: MarketPro
Text: $APLD Part II: • APLD's long-term, take-or-pay hyperscale contracts provide a level of revenue visibility that can support an AFFO-based valuation framework as the contracted capacity becomes operational. Potential Valuation Range Under the assumptions used in this analysis, the resulting valuation band is: $390 – $528 per share The range reflects different valuation methodologies, and the multiple investors ultimately assign to APLD's mature cash flows. A revenue-multiple approach values the business primarily on its top-line revenue, while an AFFO approach attempts to value the recurring cash flow generated after sustaining capital expenditures. Therefore, the $390–$528 range should be viewed as a scenario-based valuation range rather than a prediction of APLD's future share price. ________________________________________

Author: MarketPro
Text: $APLD Part III: What Is AFFO? AFFO = Adjusted Funds From Operations In the data-center REIT industry—including companies such as Equinix (EQIX) and Digital Realty (DLR)—FFO and AFFO are important metrics used by investors to evaluate operating performance and recurring cash generation. AFFO is particularly relevant for a mature data-center portfolio because it attempts to measure the cash generated by the existing assets after accounting for the expenditures necessary to maintain those assets. What AFFO Represents AFFO generally starts with Funds From Operations (FFO) and then adjusts for items such as: • Recurring/sustaining capital expenditures required to maintain the existing asset base • Straight-line rent adjustments • Non-cash items • Other company-specific normalizing adjustments The objective is to approximate the recurring cash-generating capacity of the operating portfolio after sustaining the existing assets.

Author: MarketPro
Text: $APLD Part IV: Why This Could Become Important for APLD APLD is currently in a major development and construction phase, so it should not yet be viewed as equivalent to a mature REIT such as EQIX or DLR. The important transition occurs as APLD's large development expenditures increasingly shift toward a mature portfolio requiring primarily sustaining capital. If APLD ultimately reaches a mature, contracted, REIT-like operating model—with substantial long-term hyperscale leases and relatively modest sustaining capex compared with operating cash flow—then AFFO could become a substantially more meaningful valuation metric than revenue alone. In that scenario, the valuation question becomes less about how much revenue APLD generates and more about how much recurring cash flow that revenue ultimately produces for shareholders—and what AFFO multiple the market assigns to it. Author: KavaStocks
Text: $APLD It's that time of the quarter again, so here's what I'm watching going into earnings. In July, Applied Digital put a twelve-month clock on a billion-dollar NOI run rate, and nobody made them do that. Wednesday is the first print against that clock. The headline is set up to look bad, and it should. Revenue will probably come in well below last quarter's $258.7 million, because $152.4 million of that was tenant fit-out. Fit-out runs through revenue like a contractor's invoice, at about a contractor's margin, and the CFO called it lumpy and nonrecurring back in April. The Street has this quarter at roughly half of last. Estimates have been light for two reports running, and fit-out made up most of the gap last time, so another beat wouldn't surprise me. It would mostly tell me the crews were busy. GAAP should show a loss, too. Last quarter, stock comp alone was larger than the entire net loss. The rent line is where the clock shows up first. Building 1 has paid $44.1 million in base rent two quarters in a row, which makes it the control. The first half of Building 2 went live June 30, so this quarter should carry about two months of rent from it. My rough math puts base rent around $65 million and NOI near $60 million, up from $39.9 million last quarter. A number well above that could mean some of the back half was already paying before the quarter closed, and Friday's release never said when those halls went live. With 250 megawatts live, NOI should already be running close to $400 million a year, which is well past anything this quarter can show. The billion takes something like 625 megawatts. Harwood's leased 200 and the last Ellendale building get you to 600 by next summer. That assumes the Ellendale building lands in time, and the filings only say 2027. The last stretch leans on the hundred megawatts at Harwood nobody has signed yet, or on Delta Forge arriving at the very front of its window. That makes the most important lease on Wednesday's call an unsigned one. In July, Wes said they were in advanced negotiations with two existing tenants to expand at materially higher rent, and Harwood's hundred is one of them. Ten weeks later, I'd like to hear whether advanced turned into signed. The rate matters as much as the signature, because higher rent gets more NOI out of the same capacity and gives us another read on what tenants are willing to pay. Funding is the least fun part of the release, and it decides how much of all this reaches common shareholders. Macquarie's preferred balance doubled last quarter, so the August balance sheet will show how much more capital is now sitting ahead of the common. The other half is whether the cost of new debt keeps falling the way it did on the last notes. The record going in is about as clean as it gets. Building 2 finished last week, so nobody has a delay to explain on the call. Now I want to hear Wes repeat the twelve months, with Harwood still on schedule and a firmer date on the last Ellendale building. If the rent comes through and that schedule holds, I'll take the quarter, whatever the revenue headline does. If it slips, we'll need to know why, because a late transformer and a funding problem would look identical on the calendar. Wednesday night I'll go straight to the rent line and skip the headline. Then I'll go back and look at the headline anyway, like everyone else.

Text: $APLD $BE $IYW $ORCL $QQQ @StocktwitsNews @AppliedDigital Power isn’t becoming the bottleneck. Power has been the bottleneck since roughly 2023. What’s changing is where the bottleneck sits: from power procurement to power execution. Which is why lumping APLD into this as though IO Fund just uncovered some new risk is funny. APLD’s investment case has increasingly been about conversion efficiency: contracted load → construction → RFS → rent → NOI APLD and Jupiter aren’t at the same point on that ladder. Jupiter is illustrating risk before operationalization. APLD already has live buildings producing rent and is progressively converting additional MW into paying capacity. That doesn’t eliminate execution risk. It means the risk profile is different. In 2026+, the scarce commodity isn’t just procured megawatts. It’s executable operational megawatts that pay rent. Author: marzpacker
Text: $APLD Per Gemini: Roughly 80% to 85% of daily volume in high-beta AI infrastructure stocks like Applied Digital (APLD) is driven by automated, algorithmic execution engines. These algorithms operate on quantitative models focused on short-term liquidity, which accounts for the daily price swings. Instead of evaluating multi-year growth, algorithms automatically push the stock up or down based on four primary catalysts: 10-Year Treasury Yields: Yield spikes trigger automated selling to price in higher borrowing costs, while falling yields prompt buying. Signed Master Leases: NLP bots scan headlines for long-term lease agreements with investment-grade hyperscalers to immediately de-risk cash flows. Closing Non-Dilutive Debt: Securing project-level debt without issuing new shares eliminates dilution penalties and sparks buying pressure. Megawatt Energization: Bringing online capacity into quarterly Net Operating Income (NOI) forces algorithms to re-rate forward earnings multiples.

Text: @MarketPro $APLD $RILY $BW The $2M figure needs context. That’s APLD’s ASC 321 carrying value for an illiquid 10% stake—not a market valuation of Base or evidence the stake is worth only $2M. The real catalyst is the BW guarantee: a Base exchange listing will let APLD terminate its backstop on a $2.4B project by giving notice. That is huge. The way I see this: APLD’s Base stake is the upside; the power contract is the strategy; the guarantee is the risk. The IPO could change all three. But you have to distinguish an investment from a loan receivable, and a contingent guarantee from funded debt.

Text: $APLD This is actually a much more interesting development than it first appears, because APLD managed to eliminate a potential $2.4 billion contractual exposure without waiting for Base Electron to go public! And here's the surprising part: APLD accomplished this by paying $37 million on Base Electron's behalf, rather than the $50 million termination fee originally described in its agreement. I checked APLD's SEC filings to reconcile the numbers. 1. How did APLD get out of the $2.4 billion guarantee? The original February 26, 2026 agreement with Babcock & Wilcox provided three ways APLD could terminate its guarantee. Original termination route Requirement Base Electron goes public Shares listed on a national exchange Base raises outside capital At least $50 million of qualifying financing, with payments to B&W current APLD pays a termination fee $50 million by August 1, subject to conditions, or $100 million otherwise.

Author: Multyflyer
Text: $APLD But on May 29, 2026, APLD disclosed that the guarantee was terminated upon its payment of $37 million on behalf of Base Electron. That $37 million was then added to the loan Base owes APLD. ￼ In other words, APLD and the relevant parties reached a termination arrangement that the later filing reports as effective, without Base first needing to become publicly traded. The filings establish the outcome, although they don't fully explain why $37 million was sufficient rather than the original $50 million fee. We shouldn't assume the difference was simply a negotiated discount without seeing the underlying termination agreement. The important fact is that the guarantee was terminated.

Author: 10xorbust
Text: $APLD Yes, I’ve read what’s public as part of my DD. Only the $CRWV leases have been publicly disclosed and filed with the SEC although of course they are in redacted form. The contents of the other leases have been disclosed in $APLD filings in terms of the characterizations of them. And yes, tenants CAN terminate the leases IF $APLD misses the delivery deadlines in the contracts. $CRWV and $ORCL both have that protection. There are grace periods, possible extensions and notice requirements, so missing a target date doesn’t automatically give the tenant a way out. For $CRWV’s first two leases, $APLD specifically says a qualifying delivery failure can let the tenant terminate the lease without a termination fee or further lease payments. For the remaining 150 MW building, there is a July 29, 2027 deadline for the first three halls to meet the required commencement conditions. Some of the details are redacted, so I wouldn’t pretend we can see every exception. For $ORCL, there is a cancellation right if delivery runs more than 150 days late against phased dates starting October 1, 2026. Fitch also reports an $ORCL parent guarantee and rights to terminate for chronic outages. But $ORCL’s actual agreements are not public, so I don’t know every notice requirement or exactly what $ORCL would owe when using one of those exits. For the $META projects at Delta Forge 1, Delta Forge 2 and Polaris Forge 3, I’ve read the public disclosures. I haven’t seen the actual tenant leases which are NOT available. To be clear, $APLD has never acknowledged $META as the tenant but Wells Fargo reported it, and I have reported it too from mine and other’s examinations of the publicly available filings. ￼ We know $APLD acknowledges construction-delay cancellation risk, but we don’t have those projects’ specific deadlines, exceptions or guarantee terms. I’m not going to claim I’ve reviewed clauses that haven’t been released. If a tenant simply changes its plans, that’s expensive. APLD says voluntary cancellation by the tenant requires payment of the entire remaining contract value. $CRWV’s clause is explicit: 100% of the remaining scheduled base rent, plus specified taxes, paid before the cancellation takes effect. That payment requirement is separate from its rights to terminate the lease for delivery failures, uncured $APLD defaults, major property damage or condemnation. The lease values are roughly $11B for $CRWV , $5B for $ORCL and $20.2B across the $META projects, over 15 years. Most have three optional five-year renewals; $ORCL has two. I count the roughly $36B of initial-term commitments separately from the much larger $85 billion figure that assumes every renewal gets exercised. There are also protections in the later $CRWV arrangements. Some leases moved to a subsidiary, with parent guarantees that kick in under specified circumstances. At ELN-02, if the subsidiary’s lease ends, the suspended parent lease resumes for those halls. Moving the lease into a subsidiary doesn’t, by itself, make the parent’s commitment disappear. As we all know, the KEY factor to $APLD raking in this huge pile of revenue is on time construction execution. So far, $APLD has executed its construction milestones flawlessly. There’s no guarantee $APLD will continue to do that but I’m quite optimistic given it’s spotless to date track record. $APLD already has the first 250 MW for $CRWV operating at Polaris Forge 1 and has projected completing another 600 MW within the next 12 months. These lease contracts make it expensive for tenants to change their minds, but $APLD still must finish the remaining buildings on time and keep them running as promised. I take the backlog seriously. The delivery deadlines are part of the deal too.

Text: $APLD It is very hard to time the very bottom but as $APLD has fallen to $20 and $18 I have gone in heavy and increased my position from 9000 to 25,000 shares and taken of my average down from $26 to $22.26. If it continues to fall into the $16S and $15S, which I believe it absolutely will before the before the midterms, I will continue to add by selling some of my other assets. If history is any teacher, we will have a large bounce after the midterms as historically midterm years are the best performing years of any four years of the election cycle. Stocks have historically done best in the year after the midterms. Washington Trust Bank looked at 1979 through 2023 and found that stocks in big U.S. companies returned an average of 20% that year, including dividends. The averages for the other years were 16.6% in a president’s first year, 4.7% in the midterm year, and 7.1% in the presidential election year. So the year after midterms came out ahead of all three. https://www.watrust.com/articles/understanding-us-market-returns-in-presidential-election-years Capital Group looked further back, to 1950, and found a similar result. The S&P 500 gained an average of 15.1% in the 12 months after midterm elections. That was almost twice the average gain over similar periods in other years. These are two different ways of measuring returns, but both show that stocks have tended to do well after midterms. https://www.capitalgroup.com/advisor/insights/articles/midterm-elections-markets-5-charts.html The gains have often started before the election year ends. A study in The Journal of Wealth Management found especially strong returns in the last three months of the midterm year and the first six months of the next year. This time around, that means October 2026 through June 2027. That doesn’t mean we’ll get the same result this time. Interest rates, company profits, and the economy still matter. https://ir.canterbury.ac.nz/items/eab40caf-412e-45b8-aec1-461cb2379b65 But I feel bullish about a recovery after the midterms given the strong historical pattern and the massive pre midterm selloff. Especially where $APLD has $36 billion in 15 year non-cancelable take or pay leases (over $25 billion of which is from $META and $ORCL) and has been executing on its construction deadlines flawlessly and does not have the kind of severe community opposition some of its competitors who are trying to build in datacenter heavy or anti datacenter blue states have experienced. Author: KavaStocks
Text: $APLD $CRWV $META Meta reports Wednesday, and Applied Digital and CoreWeave both have a lot riding on it. The APLD board has speculated that Meta is the customer behind the company's three newest campuses and offered some great evidence for it. The filings check out. The tenant on the Delta Forge 2 county paperwork is registered at 1 Meta Way. Applied has already said all three campuses share one customer, so more than half of its contract book would sit with Meta. It's still unofficial, which is how hyperscalers tend to like it. Meta matters on the CoreWeave side, too. It's one of CoreWeave's biggest customers, and a Meta contract backed the first investment-grade loan CoreWeave ever landed. Applied's credit work on the Ellendale leases came right behind that loan. On that side of the book, CoreWeave is the middleman. This week the market went after the middleman, and the backdrop gave it plenty of reason. The Fed went back to hiking in September, Wednesday's inflation print ran hot, and the odds of a second hike at the October 28 meeting went from about one in five to roughly a coin flip. Money rotated out of AI and chips, which is how the Dow finished the week up while the Nasdaq pulled back a week after it set a record. Oracle, the Korean memory names, and the neoclouds all sold off on worries about how the buildout gets financed and what that money costs. CoreWeave's unsecured 2031s traded as low as 78 cents on the dollar, yielding more than 16 percent, while the 10-year fell almost a quarter of a point. Rising hike odds and a falling 10-year read to me like a market pricing a Fed that tightens into a slowdown, which is a bad combination for the biggest borrower in the group. Applied's exposure runs through Ellendale. CoreWeave is the weakest credit on a tenant list where everyone else is investment grade, and its bear case was always going to live in the interest line. Last quarter that interest bill ran about five times its adjusted operating income. CoreWeave will be back in the market for money for at least the next couple of years, and the cheapest door it has left depends on rating agencies feeling generous in a tape like this. I'm not waving that off. Then I pulled up the landlord paper, which was a lot calmer. The 7 percent notes from June, the ones funding the third Ellendale building, slipped about a point to 94.5. CoreWeave is the tenant behind those notes and the borrower behind its own 2031s, yet at the lows their yields were about eight percentage points apart. Most of that gap is collateral. The Ellendale noteholders have a lien on the building and its lease, and CoreWeave needs that capacity to serve its own customers. CoreWeave's unsecured holders get paid after everyone with collateral. Cipher's secured notes, with no CoreWeave behind them, barely moved off par. That tells me the people who get paid first are pricing this as a CoreWeave problem. The stocks didn't sort any of it out. Landlords with no CoreWeave exposure got sold right alongside Applied and Galaxy, and I'd have been surprised by anything else. The landlords themselves stand about where their bonds do. If I got to pick how a credit scare in this sector plays out, I'd pick something close to this week, with the most levered name's unsecured debt taking the hit while the paper secured by buildings mostly holds. The risk I'm left with sits in the stretch where interest is already on the books and the rent is still catching up. A building slipping now gives a tenant under pressure an opening to revisit the lease, and the financing for the next campuses gets priced in this tape. If the landlord notes start following CoreWeave's unsecured debt down, the structure isn't providing the protection I'm counting on, and the bond quotes would show it well before a lease does. Meta goes first on Wednesday. If the spending holds, the money keeps moving down the line. A capex cut or softer talk about renting outside capacity would hit everyone below it, and Applied twice. The Fed meets a week later, CoreWeave reports a couple of weeks after that, and I'll read its interest line before I look at the backlog. It's an uncomfortable spot to be in. The parts of the structure I can check held up this week, and I own the equity, which is last in line behind all of it. The stock and the structure can stay out of sync for a while, and this kind of selloff will probably return every time CoreWeave raises money. I can live with that as long as the landlord notes stay where they are.

Author: KavaStocks
Text: $SPCX $APLD $NBIS SpaceX reported tonight, and for a rocket company, they spent a lot of the call talking about power. Anyone holding the AI data center names, landlords and GPU clouds alike, had reason to listen. Musk said hyperscalers and smaller firms are hounding them for capacity, with enough demand to rent out their compute several times over. Renewals are coming in at higher rates, and the CFO said new deployments pay for themselves in under a year at those prices. That is what a seller's market sounds like. They are now targeting roughly 13 gigawatts by the end of next year, well above the range they gave a few weeks ago. Musk's timelines run on Elon time, and even after a healthy haircut that is a lot of turbines. Turbines happen to be the bottleneck he named, all the way down to casting the blades and vanes. A company that builds its own rocket engines is stuck in the same equipment line as everyone else trying to energize a data center. That is the whole argument for this group, said out loud by the most aggressive builder in the business. Capacity that is already powered and running is the scarce thing, and the people who have it get to choose their customers. Where they all part ways is how they get paid. SpaceX builds its own capacity, power plants included, and rents out the compute on short terms at spot prices. It collects every bit of the upside while the shortage lasts and reprices first if it ever ends. GPU clouds like Nebius also own the chips and sell the compute, mostly through multi-year contracts with some sold on demand. Landlords like Applied Digital lease the building and the power for years, and the tenant brings the GPUs. Rising compute prices reach the GPU clouds directly, through renewals and the hours they sell on demand. For the landlords, better compute economics put more cash behind the rent, and scarce energized power strengthens their hand on the next lease. They are three ways to own the same shortage, and tonight was good for all three. That is plenty of good news for a group the market spent last week treating like a crime scene. Every fear behind that selloff was about money. People worried about too much debt, too many neoclouds for the world to keep, bond yields that look like hazard pay, and a growing suspicion that half the financing in this industry is the industry lending to itself. SpaceX is in that club too, since part of its plan relies on funding partnerships with its own vendors and customers. Tonight's call was about the other side of the ledger, with more customers than compute, prices going up, and a turbine line nobody gets to skip. The two stories connect, and that is the part the market keeps missing. Expensive money slows new construction first, and slower construction stretches out the shortage SpaceX just described. That makes capacity that already exists worth more, whether it is a powered building or a cluster that is already racked and running. Tight money still bites, and it bites hardest on whoever carries the chips and the debt. The landlords mostly feel it through their tenants, which is why the name on the lease matters as much as the megawatts. It is a real risk to this buildout and a strange reason to sell the people who already have the capacity. If you did that last week, tonight was an uncomfortable call to sit through.
